title: The Angina Eased and the Nerves Went Numb — Perhexiline Mitochondrial CPT1/CPT2 Inhibition, CYP2D6 Saturable Clearance, Phospholipidosis & Neuropathy TDM

teenKit.tldr: A powerful heart medication called perhexiline brilliantly cures chest pain by starving the heart of glucose, but it accidentally poisons the nervous system when the body fails to break it down. It is a striking medical paradox of saving one organ while quietly wrecking another.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It proves that the human body is an interconnected web rather than a collection of isolated parts, showing why modern medicine requires obsessive precision to avoid life-altering side effects.
keyTakeaways: Refractory exertional angina is a brutal condition where narrowed arteries starve the heart of oxygen during physical effort, causing agonizing chest pain.
Perhexiline acts as a metabolic switch, forcing the heart to burn fats instead of glucose, which lowers oxygen demand and stops angina.
Because people process drugs at wildly different speeds, a life-saving dose for one person can accumulate and destroy nerves, causing permanent numbness and coordination loss.

vocab.meaning: Severe, crushing chest pain caused when the heart muscle does not get enough oxygen-rich blood.
Blocking the cellular doorways that let fats into the cell's power generators, forcing a dramatic shift in how the heart creates energy.
A specific liver enzyme bottleneck that breaks down drugs, which can easily get overwhelmed and cause dangerous medicine buildup in the blood.
A strange cellular traffic jam where fats and waste products build up inside cells, eventually choking and destroying nerve tissue.

quiz.question: Why did the patient experience such intense pain in his chest during physical activity?
options: His lungs were filling up with fluid from a viral infection.
His narrowed coronary arteries could not deliver enough oxygen-rich blood to his hard-working heart muscle.
His brain was misinterpreting signals from his stomach muscles.
His nervous system was overproducing adrenaline.
quiz.explanation: Plaque-filled coronary arteries restrict blood flow, starving the myocardium of oxygen the moment it demands more energy.

quiz.question: What was the core trade-off or paradox of using perhexiline to treat this patient?
options: It cured his heart pain but instantly caused total hair loss.
It lowered his blood pressure so much that he constantly fell asleep.
It successfully eliminated his chest pain by shifting heart metabolism, but slowly accumulated to poison his nerves.
It worked great for his nerves but completely destroyed his heart function.
quiz.explanation: Perhexiline solved the immediate crisis of angina, but poor clearance caused it to build up as a quiet poison in the nervous system.

quiz.question: What does 'CYP2D6 Saturable Clearance' refer to in the context of this drug's toxicity?
options: A liver enzyme system that gets completely overwhelmed, causing the drug to pile up dangerously in the body.
An immune system reaction that attacks the drug molecules in the bloodstream.
A mechanism where the kidneys flush the medicine out too fast to work.
A special protein that helps the medicine cross the blood-brain barrier.
quiz.explanation: Saturable clearance means the liver's disposal crew gets maxed out, turning a safe dose into an accidental overdose over time.
